findings.text: The first sentence tells a newcomer plainly what Athena is. The next two lede paragraphs explain that this page is a study and why it exists, so the reader is oriented within three paragraphs.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository."

findings.text: A next-step link sits at the top of the page and jumps to the Next steps section, so the reader does not have to scroll through the whole study to find out what to do.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself"

findings.text: The install step assumes the reader already has a checkout. It gives no clone command, no prerequisites (a Rust toolchain, model access or API keys), and does not say what `athena ask` will do to the repository it runs in.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: The lede names Athena's main features, but the page never shows any of them. The study shows Athena reading code, not making a change, checking one model's work with another, or recording costs. So the case for why Athena matters rests on a side ability.
findings.source: "has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost"

findings.text: Most of the page is a detailed internal study of a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets a lot of material they don't need, and the parts about Athena are small by comparison.
findings.source: Page title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and sections States, Counters, Transitions

findings.text: Key terms are defined before they are used, which helps. Some terms still go undefined, though, such as "open captain call", "heartbeat", "endpoint", "durable record", "crewmates" and "watcher's liveness tick".
The same facts come back many times: yolo, the captain approving merges, and exit 75 against exit 1. This makes a long page longer and hides the overall picture.
findings.source: yolo is explained in "Words used first", "What firstmate is", step 5, t4, t10 and the Glossary

findings.text: A merge drawn as a move from a state back to the same state needs a long explanation before it makes sense. A first-time reader will probably find it confusing.
findings.source: t10 "ready → ready": "The task stays Ready because merging does not end it"

findings.text: This points to a folder the newcomer cannot see and gives no link to it, so it is of no use to them.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"

findings.text: The page is honest that nothing was run and that every claim comes from reading source files, which builds trust. The citation links to exact file lines at the pinned commit make that trust something the reader can check.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read"
